source.title: Sustained Gradient Alignment Mediates Subliminal Learning in a Multi-Step Setting: Evidence from MNIST Auxiliary Logit Distillation Experiment

record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly reproduces the MNIST MLP auxiliary-logit distillation experiment from the cited subliminal-learning study, using a shared teacher/student initialization and synthetic-noise distillation, and reports trait transfer and gradient-alignment results.
record.gate_note: Reports the MNIST student’s digit-classification performance, gradient alignment, and outcomes under gradient projection and liminal training. It does not test language-model text outputs or explicit filtering.
record.test_reason: It reproduces the original paper's MNIST MLP auxiliary-logit distillation experiment, with shared initialization and noise inputs. It reports trait transfer (test accuracy) and tests the gradient-alignment mechanism causally by projecting out the trait-aligned gradient component.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that sustained, weak positive trait–distillation gradient alignment mediates and causally drives trait acquisition in this multi-step MNIST setup, with the first-order effect dominant. Projection removing the trait-aligned component stops acquisition while preserving distillation. Liminal training only attenuates early alignment, delaying but not preventing final transfer. They caveat that results may not hold where higher-order effects dominate.
record.recipe_differences: Reproduces the cited MNIST MLP auxiliary-logit distillation experiment with shared initialization and synthetic-noise inputs. This paper additionally tests trait-gradient projection and liminal training; it does not study language-model text outputs.
record.method_sensitivity: Liminal training reduces alignment during the first epoch, but alignment and trait acquisition continue as regularization decays.
record.problems: The results are from one MNIST MLP setup and may not generalize where higher-order loss-landscape effects dominate. The paper notes that intervention gradient estimates use a single audit mini-batch for Figure 2A and 10 audit mini-batches for Figure 2B; the latter is not a literal full-audit estimate. Some intervention curves are described qualitatively rather than numerically.

untested.parts: Language-model students, text outputs (numbers, code, maths), filtering, and animal or preference traits. Only the MNIST MLP auxiliary-logit analogue is tested.
Entire version: teacher and student always share initialization.

Token entanglement, divergence tokens, and steering-vector directions. Only the first-order gradient-alignment argument is tested, and only in one MNIST setup; higher-order-dominated settings are explicitly not covered.
Entire version: no full fine-tuning versus LoRA comparison, no rank variation, no evaluation-prompt variation.

missing.what: Per-run final accuracy range of 26.31% to 76.04% across seeds, showing large seed variability in transfer strength.
Alignment is higher early in training, coinciding with faster trait cross-entropy decrease. The authors link this to the critical period.

record.verdict_notes: This is a workshop paper (SciForDL) with a single small MLP setup and 100 seeds. Intervention runs estimate the trait gradient from audit mini-batches (1 for Fig 2A, 10 for Fig 2B) rather than the full audit set. The liminal-training result is better read as consistent with the mechanism than as limiting it, so the reader's limits_scope label on D was replaced. Linking the MNIST analogue to version A is debatable because the version names text outputs. It is kept because the original paper presents this experiment as an instance of the phenomenon.

versions.untested_parts: Tests MNIST digit-classification trait transfer through auxiliary-logit distillation on synthetic noise, not favourite-animal traits, text outputs, or a textual filtering procedure.
Teacher and student share an identical initialization throughout; no different-base comparison is reported.
No misalignment or other alignment-relevant trait is tested.
Tests gradient alignment and removal of its trait-aligned component in this MNIST setup, not token entanglement, divergence tokens, or a steering-vector-like direction.
No full-fine-tuning versus LoRA-rank comparison or evaluation-prompt variation is tested.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens is tested.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on transfer in the MNIST analogue and on the gradient-alignment mechanism.

tranche.reason: Reproduces the original's MNIST MLP auxiliary-logit distillation (shared initialization, uniform-noise inputs, test accuracy). It adds mechanism tests (gradient projection, liminal training).

source_check.notes: Short SciForDL workshop paper. The ± values are most likely SD across 100 seeds (per the figure captions); per-run final accuracy ranges from 26.31% to 76.04%. For the intervention runs the trait gradient is approximated: one audit mini-batch for Fig. 2A, ten for Fig. 2B. There is no different-initialization control, and teacher accuracy is not reported.

statements.problem: For this study, 55.28 ± 10.48%, 48.97 ± 9.63% and 100 seeds are all in the text. 'About 10% chance' is inferred from the 10 classes; the text only says 'above-chance' and calls 10.14% 'near-chance'.
Says nothing specific about this study. Leaving it out of the peer-reviewed list fits its review class, 'other' (SciForDL workshop).
All numbers match Sections 3.1-3.2. A minor omission: the projection is applied only on steps with a positive inner product.
Correct. This study uses shared initialization only and never varies it, so it does not bear on whether shared initialization is needed.
'Reproduced and extended' is fair. The study tests the single-step theorem's prediction empirically in multi-step training and adds a causal projection test; it does not re-derive the theorem.
